source.title: Scaling laws for decoding images from brain activity
source.authors: Hubert J. Banville; Yohann Benchetrit; Stéphane d'Ascoli; Jérémy Rapin; Jean-Rémi King

record.tranche_reason: The study extends scaling analyses to brain-to-image decoding from EEG, MEG and fMRI recordings; it does not study language-model pretraining loss.
record.gate_note: The study measures image-embedding decoding performance, not language-model held-out cross-entropy or image/video model pretraining loss. It reports its own scaling outcomes for training-recording quantity and number of subjects. The linear-versus-deep comparisons and reconstruction results do not test the claim versions.
record.test_reason: The study fits data-scaling trends for brain-to-image decoders, a non-text setting. That bears on V5 only loosely: the measure is test Pearson R of predicted DINOv2 embeddings, fitted log-linearly, not a power law in held-out loss.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct. The authors find no plateau: decoding R scales log-linearly with recording quantity. Within-subject data drives the gain, while adding subjects gives modest or no improvement.
record.recipe_differences: This is a brain-to-image decoding benchmark, not a language-model loss-scaling experiment. It varies the amount of brain recordings and subjects and measures Pearson correlation of predicted image embeddings.
record.method_sensitivity: The fitted log-linear slopes depend on recording device; gains also differ between increasing within-subject recordings and adding subjects. Dataset and experimental-protocol differences are noted by the authors.

fits_no_version.finding: Averaging over more test-time repetitions raises decoding R with diminishing, log-linear returns (Spearman 0.33-0.97 across devices).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Test-time signal averaging improves brain decoding with diminishing returns.

record.problems: The evidence concerns brain-decoding correlation rather than language-model loss. The authors note that datasets differ in image sets and experimental paradigms, and that these differences may affect performance. Several dataset-specific trends are presented graphically without numeric values in the text.
record.rows_left_out: Not applicable; all numerical device-level recording-hour slopes stated in Section 3.7 and the explicitly described subject-count outcomes were recorded.

untested.parts: Scaling with model size or compute (the authors call larger architectures an open question). Whether loss, rather than Pearson R, follows a power law. Image/video generative pretraining, repeated data, fine-tuning and transfer.
No extrapolation test. Cost-based predictions are in-range fits, not validated on larger runs.

missing.what: Per-dataset slopes of R versus log(hours): values 0.030, 0.023, 0.045, 0.064, 0.039, 0.048, 0.051, 0.075, whose dataset mapping is unclear from the text.
Within-subject trial scaling: trials needed to reach R=0.01 (57 for 7T, 123-522 for 3T, 2.3K for MEG, ~5K for EEG).

record.verdict_notes: This fits V5 only by analogy. There is no loss measure and no model-size or compute axis, and the fitted form is log-linear performance rather than a power law. Researchers may reasonably treat it as only adjacent to V5.

versions.untested_parts: Language-model held-out pretraining loss scaling with parameter count, tokens or compute.
Whether small-run fits predict much larger language-model runs.
Architecture-shape effects at fixed parameter count.

The study tests scaling of brain-to-image decoding performance with recording quantity, not pretraining loss; it does not test image/video model pretraining, repeated-data training, fine-tuning or transfer.
Downstream task performance as a function of language-model scale or pretraining loss.
Dependence of language-model scaling exponents or compute-optimal splits on fitting choices and setup.

rows.subject: EEG decoding models (device-level fit)
rows.operation_detail: Fit decoding performance against recording duration while varying training-data quantity.
rows.measure: Slope of log-linear fit for Pearson R versus log(recording time)
rows.note: The reported scaling outcome is decoding correlation, not pretraining loss.
rows.check: The trend is log-linear in decoding correlation, not a power law in loss. It pools single-subject, matched-trial and all-trial models, so data quantity is mixed with subject count.

source_check.correct: Slope = 0.045 ± 0.003 SEM; state = cannot_determine for V5; version link = none. Log-linear scaling of Pearson R does not establish power-law scaling.
source_check.problem: The value is correct, but observed does not fit V5's power-law claim.

rows.subject: Grootswagers2022 EEG decoding models
rows.operation_detail: Compare decoding performance when doubling the number of training subjects.
rows.value: Improvement of 0.004 from doubling the number of subjects to 48; not significant (two-sided t-test, p = 0.49)
rows.note: The reported improvement was explicitly described as not significant.
rows.check: The subject axis confounds added data with inter-subject variability. The +0.004 gain is non-significant (p=0.49).

source_check.correct: Doubling subjects from 24 to 48 improves Pearson R by 0.004; two-sided t-test p = 0.49. State = cannot_determine for V5; version link = none.
source_check.problem: The non-significant gain is correctly reported, but it does not test V5's power-law form.

relationships.condition: Brain-to-image decoders trained on increasing hours of recording, within each device (EEG, MEG, 3T fMRI, 7T fMRI)
relationships.reason: All four devices show positive log-linear slopes of R versus log(hours) with no plateau (r1-r4). The form is log-linear in correlation rather than a power law in loss.
relationships.display_finding: All four devices show increasing correlation versus log recording hours without a plateau, establishing a log-linear correlation trend rather than a loss power law.

relation.reason: Section 4.1 discusses scaling laws and cites parameter/data scaling work, but the study's own correlation fits neither test nor use the catalog's power-law findings.

tranche.reason: The study fits log-linear decoding correlation against data quantity, a related construct that does not test the power-law form required by V5 or another listed version.

source_check.notes: The authors' summary of within-subject gains and limited across-subject gains is accurate. Figure 7 pools single-subject, matched-trial and all-trial regimes; the possible decreases in r6-r7 are explicitly mentioned in the text.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: Training-recording quantity in the tested device groups, using recording hours as the data axis
reader_labels.reason: The study reports log-linear increases in decoding performance with training data and positive fitted slopes for all four device groups (r1-r4); this supports an analogous scaling pattern, not a claim about pretraining loss.

reader_labels.reason: The additional benefit was small and not significant for Grootswagers2022, and performance could decrease in two 3T fMRI datasets (r5-r7).
